Scotland. A country that comprises the northern part of the island of Great Britain and over 790 adjacent islands, part of the United Kingdom since 1707. Historically distinct from England, Scotland has preserved its own legal system, educational institutions, and cultural traditions rooted in Gaelic and Norse heritage. A nation of rugged highlands, dramatic coastlines, and a long history of resistance to English dominion, Scotland has produced world-changing philosophers, scientists, and innovations.

Scotland's geography is divided into the Highlands to the northwest, the Lowlands in the south and central regions, and the Southern Uplands. It is home to Loch Ness, famous for legends of its monster. William Wallace and Robert the Bruce led Scottish resistance to English conquest in the late 13th and early 14th centuries, culminating in the Declaration of Arbroath in 1320 asserting Scottish independence.

The Scottish Enlightenment in the 18th century was a flowering of intellectual achievement that produced philosophers like David Hume and Adam Smith, whose ideas shaped modern political economy and philosophy. Gaelic and Scots languages are indigenous to Scotland. Though historically suppressed, they have experienced a cultural revival, and Gaelic is now taught in schools alongside English.

The Highland Clearances from the 18th to 19th centuries forcibly displaced thousands of crofters from the Highlands to make way for sheep farming, fundamentally altering Scottish society and spurring emigration to North America. Scotland joined with England to form the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1707 through the Acts of Union, which many Scots saw as an end to independence. Devolution in 1999 restored a Scottish Parliament.

Scottish inventors and scientists contributed enormously to the Industrial Revolution. James Watt developed the steam engine, and Alexander Graham Bell invented the telephone. Scottish culture, including tartan, bagpipes, whisky, and the Highland games, has become iconic symbols recognized worldwide.
